headline: Bangladesh holds presidential election today after 35 years; MPs to elect 23rd President
summary: The election, featuring BNP's Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir and 11-party alliance's Oli Ahmad, marks only the second time MPs will directly vote for a president since 1991.
details: Bangladesh is set to hold its presidential election today, marking the first direct vote in nearly 35 years. Members of Parliament (MPs) will elect the country's 23rd president from 2 PM to 5 PM in the Jatiya Sangsad (National Parliament) chamber.

The two candidates vying for the top post are Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir, representing the BNP, and Oli Ahmad, candidate of the 11-party alliance. A total of 349 MPs are eligible to cast their votes.
Three transparent ballot boxes will be arranged in the parliament chamber for the voting process. MPs will cast their ballots according to a prescribed method, depositing them into the boxes.
Following the voting, ballots will be counted within the parliament chamber. The Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) A.M.M. Nasir Uddin, acting as the electoral officer, will announce the results.

The Election Commission (EC) is expected to publish a gazette notification today itself. The newly elected president is scheduled to take the oath of office on Friday evening, August 21, at Bangabhaban's Darbar Hall.

The parliamentary system was reintroduced in 1991, leading to the first presidential election that year. Subsequently, the next seven presidents were elected unopposed, making this the second time MPs will directly vote.

headline_marked: [[Farmers face fertilizer shortage]] and higher prices in Bangladesh, impacting Aman paddy cultivation
headline: Farmers face fertilizer shortage and higher prices in Bangladesh, impacting Aman paddy cultivation
summary: Farmers across various districts are struggling to obtain essential fertilizers like urea and DAP at government-fixed prices, with many reporting shortages and black market sales.
details: Farmer Bablu from Godagari, Rajshahi, cultivating 10 bighas of Aman paddy, couldn't get urea from his local dealer. He waited in a long queue at a dealer in a nearby market but was only offered 20 kg, which he refused out of frustration.

Farmers like Bablu are flocking to government-appointed dealers for fertilizers needed for Aman paddy. Across Rajshahi, dealers often lack specific types of fertilizer, and where available, prices are higher than government rates.

Similar issues are reported in Jashore, with a shortage of TSP fertilizer and complaints of other fertilizers being sold at inflated prices in the open market. The Rajshahi Agriculture Extension Department admits to some shortage due to lower-than-demand allocation.

Farmers allege that government-appointed dealers are selling subsidized fertilizers to the black market, leading to artificial scarcity and higher prices. This fertilizer is then resold at inflated rates in the open market.

In response, four dealers in four Rajshahi sub-districts were fined a total of BDT 85,000 over three days for allegedly smuggling fertilizer between areas. In Jashore, two dealers were fined BDT 10,500 on August 2 for selling fertilizer at higher prices.

Rajshahi District Fertilizer and Seed Monitoring Committee President and DC Kazi Shahidul Islam claims there is sufficient fertilizer in Rajshahi. He denies knowledge of lower allocations but states mobile courts are taking immediate legal action against overpricing or smuggling.

However, sources from the Rajshahi Agriculture Extension Department reveal that the requested fertilizer allocation is rarely met. For the 2025-26 fiscal year, 305,543 metric tons of urea were demanded, but only 71,109 metric tons were allocated.
Similar significant shortfalls were observed for TSP, DAP, and MOP fertilizers. For the 2026-27 fiscal year, 77,470 metric tons of urea were demanded, but 71,109 metric tons were received.

For August, Rajshahi was allocated 7,574 metric tons of urea, but only 4,724 metric tons were received by August 18. Similar shortfalls were noted for DAP, TSP, and MOP, with only a fraction of the allocated amounts received.

In Jashore, the target for Aman cultivation is 132,692 hectares. For August, the district was allocated 3,082 MT of TSP, 2,782 MT of DAP, 2,631 MT of MOP, and 10,704 MT of urea. By Tuesday, significant portions of these allocations had been collected.

Rajshahi district has 83,600 hectares under Aman cultivation this season. The DAP allocation per bigha is approximately 4.2 kg, significantly less than the ideal application of 10 kg per bigha recommended by agricultural officials.

Furthermore, there is no fertilizer allocation for the 17,774 hectares of ponds in the district, despite a quarterly demand of 1,991 metric tons of DAP for them. This further strains the allocation for crops.
The Aman season runs from early July to mid-October, with transplanting from mid-July to August 31. TSP, DAP, and MOP are applied during transplanting, while urea is used afterward.

Mohammad Nasir Uddin, Deputy Director of Rajshahi District Agriculture Extension Department, confirmed to Prothom Alo that allocations are consistently less than requested and that pond fertilizer is not included in their quotas.
